title: The shared universe of amateurs
text: Fan fiction — stories written by amateurs about characters they do not own — is either the embarrassment or the {{1}} of modern fandom, depending on whom you ask. What is not disputed is its {{2}}: a single popular franchise can inspire millions of stories, most written for nothing, read by communities that {{3}} as critics, editors and cheerleaders. The form has its own conventions: long summaries, warnings about content, and a habit of {{4}} that would horrify a traditional publisher — unfinished stories simply stop, and readers thank the author anyway. Mainstream literature has learned to stop sneering. Publishing houses scout fan writers, whose {{5}} of writing millions of words for free audiences turns out to be the best possible {{6}}; several best-selling series began as other people's characters, legally {{7}} into originals. The lawyers keep the {{8}} precise — fan works exist in a grey zone of parody and private enjoyment — but the cultural verdict is in: the audience stopped waiting for permission to tell stories long ago.

gaps.explanation: 'either the embarrassment or the engine of fandom' — what powers it; enigma = a puzzle.
'what is not disputed is its scale' — how big it is; scalpel = a surgeon's knife.
'communities that act as critics, editors and cheerleaders' — perform the functions; pose as implies pretence, and vote and cheer are not the roles listed.
'a habit of abandonment — unfinished stories simply stop' — giving up mid-way; amendment = a small change to a text.
'whose apprenticeship of writing millions of words for free' — their unpaid training period; enticement = a temptation.
'the best possible preparation' — training for what came next; prescription = a doctor's instruction.
'legally transformed into originals' — changed into something new; transpire = turn out or leak out.
'the lawyers keep the distinctions precise' — the fine legal lines; distraction = something that takes attention away.
